extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and informed readers of political theory and comparative government (esp. readers of Democracy in America)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles and evaluative standards for judging the effects of centralization vs local administration in democracies, and the nature and political role of the judiciary (including judicial review). Geared toward comparative analysis of political institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of absent centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of a central government produces divided control, prevents obedience to general laws, leads to members refusing co-operation with central representatives, and impedes nations from advancing with energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: feudal Middle Ages, where control was divided amongst many hands; lack of a central administration causes confusion and prevents straightforward national progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local authority extent carries benefits and disadvantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Local authority in the United States has been carried to lengths which no European nation could endure without great inconvenience, and which has even produced some disadvantageous consequences in America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While local administration fosters civic activity and is often preferable, it may produce inconveniences (e.g., slow tax collection) and prevent the execution of undertakings important to the whole State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative supremacy within States
rubrics_metrics.description: In America the legislature of each State is supreme; nothing can impede its authority; its own determination is the only limit to its action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This central political concentration within states makes national power compact even while local administration is pervasive; district assemblies and county courts are not multiplied so as to avoid interference with government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should employ its own removable officers for material matters
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable that, in whatever materially affects its existence, the Government should be served by officers of its own, appointed by itself, removable at pleasure, and accustomed to rapid methods of proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local methods (e.g., assessor, collector, town-treasurer) of tax collection are slow and inconvenient; a central government organized as in America can nonetheless introduce more efficacious modes when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local administration leads to lack of uniform police/regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the State has no administrative functionaries of its own stationed across its territory, it rarely attempts to issue general police regulations; the want of such regulations is severely felt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: undertakings important to the whole State often cannot be executed because there is no national administration to direct them; efforts left to towns/counties lead to no durable benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central authority should inspect local administration without active interference
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority which represents the State ought not to waive the right of inspecting the local administration, even when it does not interfere more actively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested remedy: station an agent of the Government to prosecute misdemeanors of town and county officers to produce more uniform order while preserving township independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization excels at routine and prevention but stifles innovation and citizen cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralization imparts admirable regularity to routine business, represses small disorders, and maintains society in a status quo secure from improvement and decline; but its force deserts it when society is to be disturbed or accelerated, or when private co-operation is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralization succeeds in external uniformity and administrative details, yet it cannot embrace all details of a great nation; when it requires private citizens' free and responsible action, it becomes impotent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect central administration yields stability without improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A completely central administration may furnish peace without happiness, industry without improvement, stability without strength, and public order without public morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: China is given as the exemplar: tolerable social condition but never excellent; centralization can produce order at the cost of progress and public virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local system fosters energetic civic activity and public welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Local institutions produce a power which, though somewhat barbarous, is robust; citizens make large exertions for the common weal: abundant schools, effective places of worship, well-kept roads, and private undertakings that in aggregate exceed what the State might have accomplished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although local budgets may be chaotic, the end of good government is welfare, not mere order; American townships show activity, information, and enterprise even where accounts lack uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizens’ sense of ownership vs state-provided services
rubrics_metrics.description: When government monopolizes administration, citizens become indifferent to local affairs and lack tendencies to obedience except before petty officers; they surrender interest and ownership of local improvements to a distant authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resulting civic passivity leaves communities vulnerable to despotism or decline; conversely, local responsibility encourages improvement and care.

rubrics_metrics.name: In democracies, provincial institutions are indispensable
rubrics_metrics.description: Provincial institutions are most indispensable among a democratic people: a democracy without provincial institutions has no security against despotism and no place for citizens to learn and practice moderation in small concerns before larger affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristocracies have other checks; democracies need local institutions to provide ties between citizens and to build resistance to tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic tendency toward centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic nations tend to concentrate governmental strength in the hands of the power which represents the people, because beyond the people there is nothing but a mass of equal individuals; such concentration predisposes to centralization and eventual penetration into administrative details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: French Revolution combined impulses toward liberty and despotism, producing centralization that ultimately undermined provincial institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: American obedience is to law/justice rather than to persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The European generally submits to a public officer because he represents a superior force; to an American, an officer represents a right; obedience is rendered to justice and law, not to the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fosters civic confidence and readiness to undertake projects for the common good without relying on government assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate effect of private undertakings can exceed state provision
rubrics_metrics.description: When private individuals publish plans, offer to execute them, and court others' assistance, the sum of these private undertakings often far exceeds all that the Government could have done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although individual projects may be less successful than state action in isolation, their aggregate contribution benefits the public more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen involvement can substitute for a powerful centralized police
rubrics_metrics.description: Even with few state police, the discovery and arrest of criminals can be effective because every one conceives himself interested in furnishing evidence and stopping the delinquent; spontaneous citizen committees may form to pursue and prosecute criminals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with Europe: population as mere spectators; in America the whole community acts against criminals, making crime rarely evade punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three essential characteristics of judicial power
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial power is characterized by (1) duty of arbitration (must have contested rights/causes), (2) pronouncing on special cases rather than general principles, and (3) inability to act unless appealed to—the judiciary is passive until brought into action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a judge pronounces on law without a case he invades the legislative sphere; attacking a law should occur within the context of deciding a particular dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial right to found decisions on the constitution (judicial review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans have acknowledged the right of judges to found their decisions on the constitution rather than on the laws, i.e., to refuse to apply laws they deem unconstitutional; this right is recognized and uncontested in America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification: the American constitution is the origin of authority and cannot be modified by ordinary law; judicial selection of the stricter legal obligation (constitution) is natural for a magistrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution as supreme law with amendability limits judicial danger
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the American constitution can be altered by the people via established rules, judges interpreting it do not become permanent sovereigns; the people can change the constitution, reducing the danger of judicial usurpation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with France (constitution treated as immutable) and England (Parliament as constituent), where judicial assertion of constitutional primacy would have different consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that judicial censorship of laws occur through concrete cases limits political abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Connecting the censorship of laws with private interests and requiring attacks on laws to proceed through courts in particular cases protects legislation from wanton assailants and party spirit, because the judge's decision bears upon specific interests and is less visible to public passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: laws lose moral cogency when repeatedly refused in cases, but their final destruction requires repeated judicial attacks or constitutional amendment; this process exposes legislators' errors where their consequences are felt.
